apache-parquet.wrapped_text:
Apache Parquet
What is a Parquet file, and why
does it store each column
together? [Apache Parquet](https:/
/parquet.apache.org/) is a file
format for the rows and columns of
one table. It stores the values of
each column next to each other,
not row by row. The file also
holds the column names and types.
[Apache
Iceberg](../iceberg/iceberg.md)
uses it as its usual data file
format. Snowflake supports Iceberg
tables that use Parquet files
([Snowflake documentation](https:/
/docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/
tables-iceberg)).

Keeping a column together gives
three gains. A reader loads only
the columns that a query needs.
The writer stores each column in a
compact form. A reader skips whole
blocks of rows, by using the
minimum and maximum values in the
footer. How Much Columnar Saves
measures the gains. The price is
that one row is spread over every
column. An engine, which is a
program that runs queries such as
Snowflake, also writes each
Parquet file once and replaces it
to change data. Files Are Written
Once explains why.

A reader skips whole blocks of rows, by using the minimum and maximum values in the footer. How Much Columnar Saves measures the gains. The price is that one row is spread over every column. An engine, which is a program that runs queries such as Snowflake, also writes each Parquet file once and replaces it to change data. Files Are Written Once explains why.

what-is-parquet.wrapped_text:
What Is Parquet?
A Parquet file stores the data of one table:
named, typed columns and many rows. This map
follows one example table with the columns
`id`, `city`, and `fare`, and six rows: `1,
Perth, 12.5`; `2, Perth, 8.0`; `3, Sydney,
20.0`; `4, Sydney, 15.5`; `5, Perth, 9.0`; and
`6, Perth, 11.0`. A short script writes the
table to the file `trips.parquet`, which takes
1,595 bytes. The file is stored beside this
map, and About the Numbers shows the script.
The file also stores the type of each column:
`id` is an integer (`int64`), `city` is text
(`string`), and `fare` is a decimal number
(`double`). The file stores each value as the
bytes of its number or text. With plain
encoding, which writes each value as it is,
the number 12.5 is the 8 bytes `00 00 00 00 00
00 29 40`. The writer of `trips.parquet` also
compresses the bytes with SNAPPY, a
compression method, so the file holds their
compressed form (Compress the Bytes explains
it). A CSV file stores the same number as the
four characters `12.5`, which are the bytes
`31 32 2e 35`. A tool that reads Parquet
decodes the bytes into rows and columns.

why-parquet-exists.wrapped_text:
Why Parquet Exists
The [specification](https://github.com/apache/
parquet-format/blob/ec90dd4/README.md#L34-L43)
states four goals:

- A compressed, efficient columnar
representation of data.
- Very efficient compression and encoding,
chosen for each column.
- Support for complex nested data structures.
- One format that every data processing
framework can use.

The first two goals are about cost: fewer
bytes to store and fewer bytes to read. [How
Much Columnar Saves](#how-much-columnar-saves)
measures them. The other two goals are about
what a file can hold and who can read it.

row-layout.wrapped_text:
Row Layout
A row layout stores one record after another.
A CSV (comma-separated values) file is the
usual example. The example table becomes six
text lines: `1,Perth,12.5`, then
`2,Perth,8.0`, then `3,Sydney,20.0`, and so
on. The three values of one record sit next to
each other. To read only `fare`, a reader must
scan every line and cut out the third value.
row-layout.wrapped_original_text:
Row Layout

The example table becomes six text lines: `1,Perth,12.5`, then `2,Perth,8.0`, then `3,Sydney,20.0`, and so on. The three values of one record sit next to each other. To read only `fare`, a reader must scan every line and cut out the third value.

column-layout.wrapped_text:
Column Layout
A column layout stores all values of one
column together. A Python dictionary shows the
idea. Each key is a column, and each value is
the list of that column's values. [pyarrow](ht
tps://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/generated/p
yarrow.Table.html#pyarrow.Table.to_pydict) is
the Python library for Apache Arrow. Its
`to_pydict()` method returns the example table
as `{'id': [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], 'city':
['Perth', 'Perth', 'Sydney', 'Sydney',
'Perth', 'Perth'], 'fare': [12.5, 8.0, 20.0,
15.5, 9.0, 11.0]}`. A Parquet file adds one
detail. It cuts each list into pieces, one for
each row group.

many-files-form-one-table.wrapped_text:
Many Files Form One Table
A large table is usually many Parquet files.
Each file has its own footer, which describes
only that file. A table format such as Apache
Iceberg records which files form the table. A
Snowflake Iceberg table is an example. Its
rows sit in many Parquet files in cloud
storage, and the Iceberg metadata names the
files. The [Iceberg
map](../iceberg/iceberg.md) explains the table
format, and the [Iceberg in Snowflake map](../
snowflake/iceberg/snowflake-iceberg.md) covers
Snowflake's side.

file-anatomy.wrapped_text:
File Anatomy
A Parquet file is a stack of
parts. At the top level, the file
holds row groups and a footer. A
row group holds one column chunk
for each column. A column chunk
holds pages. The picture shows the
example file down to the column
chunks, with the real byte range
of each part. The [format specific
ation](https://github.com/apache/p
arquet-format/blob/ec90dd4/README.
md#L64-L85) defines the same
hierarchy.

magic-bytes.wrapped_text:
Magic Bytes
Every Parquet file starts and ends with the
four bytes `PAR1`. A reader checks them to
know that the file is Parquet. The next bytes
start the header of the first page. In the
example file, the first 11 bytes are
`b'PAR1\x15\x04\x150\x15.L'` in Python
notation. The bytes `0x15` and `0x04` are
control codes, which an editor does not show
as letters. The [specification](https://github
.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/ec90dd4/README
.md#L92-L121) shows the layout.

row-group.wrapped_text:
Row Group
A row group is a slice of consecutive rows.
The example file has two: rows 1 to 3, and
rows 4 to 6. Read back with pyarrow, each
column shows as two pieces, one for each row
group: `id: [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]`. A row group
holds one column chunk for each column. The [s
pecification](https://github.com/apache/parque
t-format/blob/ec90dd4/README.md#L251-L257)
recommends large row groups, from 512 MB to 1
GB. Large row groups allow large sequential
reads, but the writer needs more memory. The
example uses three rows per group only to keep
the picture small.

column-chunk.wrapped_text:
Column Chunk
A column chunk holds the values of one column
inside one row group, in one contiguous byte
range. In the example file, the `id` chunk of
row group 0 covers bytes 4 to 114. The `city`
chunk follows it at bytes 114 to 196. The [spe
cification](https://github.com/apache/parquet-
format/blob/ec90dd4/README.md#L87-L90) names
the column chunk as the unit for input and
output.

The `city` chunk follows it at bytes 114 to 196. The [specification](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/ec90dd4/README.md#L87-L90) names the column chunk as the unit for input and output.

page.wrapped_text:
Page
A column chunk is a run of pages. A page is
the smallest unit that the writer encodes and
compresses ([glossary](https://github.com/apac
he/parquet-format/blob/ec90dd4/README.md#L79-L
81)). A reader can skip pages that it does not
need. When a chunk uses dictionary encoding,
its first page is the dictionary page. The
data pages follow ([specification](https://git
hub.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/ec90dd4/REA
DME.md#L207-L218)). In the example file, the
`id` chunk of row group 0 has a dictionary
page at byte 4 and a data page at byte 41.
page.wrapped_original_text:

A column chunk is a run of pages. A page is the smallest unit that the writer encodes and compresses ([glossary](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/ec90dd4/README.md#L79-L81)). A reader can skip pages that it does not need. When a chunk uses dictionary encoding, its first page is the dictionary page. The data pages follow ([specification](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/ec90dd4/README.md#L207-L218)). In the example file, the `id` chunk of row group 0 has a dictionary page at byte 4 and a data page at byte 41.

footer.wrapped_text:
Footer
The footer is the last part of the file. After
it come its length (4 bytes) and the closing
`PAR1` (4 bytes). In the example file, the
footer covers bytes 606 to 1,587. The footer
holds three things:

- The schema, which lists the column names and
types ([file metadata](https://github.com/apac
he/parquet-format/blob/ec90dd4/src/main/thrift
/parquet.thrift#L1422-L1445)).
- The byte range, codec, and encodings of
every column chunk ([column metadata](https://
github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/ec90dd4/
src/main/thrift/parquet.thrift#L922-L959)).
- The minimum and maximum value of every
column chunk.

A reader starts here. It reads the end of the
file, finds the footer length, and then reads
the footer. The writer puts the footer last,
so that it can write the file in one pass ([sp
ecification](https://github.com/apache/parquet
-format/blob/ec90dd4/README.md#L109-L121)).

why-columnar-pays.wrapped_text:
Why Columnar Pays
A query costs the bytes it reads
and the values it decodes. A row
layout keeps the fields of one row
together, so a query that needs
one column still reads every
field. A column layout keeps the
values of one column together, so
a reader fetches only the columns
that it needs.

how-much-columnar-saves.wrapped_text:
How Much Columnar Saves
The measurements use one table of 300,000 rows
with the columns `id`, `city`, `fare`, and
`note`. The table is stored three ways. CSV is
a row layout in a text file. SQLite is a row
layout in a database file, with `id` as the
primary key. Parquet is the column layout. The
three nodes below hold the numbers. About the
Numbers describes the files and the method.
how-much-columnar-saves.wrapped_original_text:
How Much Columnar Saves
The measurements use one table of 300,000 rows with the columns `id`, `city`, `fare`, and `note`. The table is stored three ways. CSV is a row layout in a text file. SQLite is a row layout in a database file, with `id` as the primary key. Parquet is the column layout. The three nodes below hold the numbers. About the Numbers describes the files and the method.

three-queries.wrapped_text:
Three Queries on One Table
The times are the median of 5 runs on one
thread, with the files in the operating system
cache. They show CPU work and no disk delay.
The byte counts are exact.

- Sum of `fare` where `city` is `Perth`. This
needs 2 of the 4 columns. Parquet reads
705,192 bytes and takes 4.5 ms. SQLite takes
12 ms. CSV reads 19,625,110 bytes and takes 23
ms.
- Sum of `fare` where `id` is at least 200000.
This needs 2 columns from 1 of the 3 row
groups. Parquet reads 866,416 bytes and takes
0.6 ms. SQLite takes 2.7 ms. CSV reads
19,625,110 bytes and takes 21 ms.
- Read every column of every row. Parquet
reads 15,416,992 bytes and takes 9.8 ms. CSV
reads 19,625,110 bytes and takes 25 ms.

In the first query, Parquet reads 28 times
fewer bytes than CSV. Two steps make the gap.
The CSV text of `city` and `fare` alone takes
4,736,208 bytes, which is 4.1 times fewer than
the whole file. Parquet stores those two
columns in 639,656 bytes, and the footer read
adds 65,536 bytes. Column Pruning, Encoding
and Compression, and Row Group Skipping
explain the steps. In the third query, Parquet
is still 2.6 times faster.

savings-grow-with-width.wrapped_text:
Savings Grow With Table Width
The gain depends on how many columns a query
skips. Each table here has 100,000 rows of
random decimal numbers, and each query sums
the first column. Parquet reads the same
334,234 bytes for every table, because the
other columns are skipped.

- 4 columns: the CSV file has 2,312,335 bytes,
which is 6.9 times more than Parquet reads.
Parquet takes 0.2 ms and CSV takes 4.2 ms.
- 20 columns: the CSV file has 11,561,921
bytes, which is 35 times more. Parquet takes
0.3 ms and CSV takes 17 ms.
- 100 columns: the CSV file has 57,805,429
bytes, which is 173 times more. Parquet takes
0.4 ms and CSV takes 85 ms.

A wide table with a narrow query gains the
most. Snowflake tables also store columns
separately, so a Snowflake query scans only
the columns that it references (see Column
Pruning).

column-pruning.wrapped_text:
Column Pruning
A reader fetches only the column chunks that a
query needs. It finds their byte ranges in the
footer and skips the rest. The test file
`trips_big.parquet` has 300,000 rows and
15,353,361 bytes (About the Numbers describes
it). A read of `fare` alone pulls 629,235
bytes, which is 4.1% of the file. A wrapper
that logged every read showed what pyarrow
18.1.0 did in November 2026. It first read the
last 64 KB of the file, which holds the
footer. It then made three reads of about 188
KB each, one for each row group, at the byte
ranges that the footer lists. It skipped the
other 14,724,126 bytes. A read of all four
columns pulled 15,416,992 bytes: every byte of
the file except the first 4, plus 63,635 bytes
that the footer read repeats. Snowflake stores
the columns of each micro-partition, its unit
of table storage, independently. A query scans
only the columns that it references ([micro-pa
rtitions](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-g
uide/tables-clustering-micropartitions)).

encoding-and-compression.wrapped_text:
Encoding and Compression
The writer prepares each page in two steps. It
first encodes the values into a compact form,
by using the type and the pattern of the
column. It then compresses the encoded bytes
with a codec, which is a compression method
that works on any bytes. A codec replaces a
repeated run of bytes with a short reference
to its first copy, and it can give common
bytes shorter bit codes. The first step works
well because a chunk holds one kind of value.
encoding-and-compression.wrapped_original_text:
Encoding and Compression
The writer prepares each page in two steps. It first encodes the values into a compact form, by using the type and the pattern of the column. It then compresses the encoded bytes with a codec, which is a compression method that works on any bytes. A codec replaces a repeated run of bytes with a short reference to its first copy, and it can give common bytes shorter bit codes. The first step works well because a chunk holds one kind of value.

encode-values.wrapped_text:
Encode the Values
Dictionary encoding stores each different value
once, in the dictionary page. The data pages then
hold small codes that point into the dictionary ([s
pecification](https://github.com/apache/parquet-for
mat/blob/ec90dd4/README.md#L213-L218)). The `city`
column of the test file has 300,000 values but only
four different names. Written as plain values, the
column takes 3,299,981 bytes. With dictionary
encoding, it takes 75,933 bytes, which is 43 times
smaller. That is about 2 bits for each row.
encode-values.wrapped_original_text:
Encode the Values
Dictionary encoding stores each different value once, in the dictionary page. The data pages then hold small codes that point into the dictionary ([specification](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/ec90dd4/README.md#L213-L218)). The `city` column of the test file has 300,000 values but only four different names. Written as plain values, the column takes 3,299,981 bytes. With dictionary encoding, it takes 75,933 bytes, which is 43 times smaller. That is about 2 bits for each row.

compress-bytes.wrapped_text:
Compress the Bytes
The writer then compresses each page with a codec (
[specification](https://github.com/apache/parquet-f
ormat/blob/ec90dd4/Compression.md#L26-L29)), and
the footer records the codec of each chunk. Every
chunk in the example file uses SNAPPY, which is the
default codec in pyarrow ([`write_table`](https://a
rrow.apache.org/docs/python/generated/pyarrow.parqu
et.write_table.html)). SNAPPY helps when bytes
repeat ([format](https://github.com/google/snappy/b
lob/main/format_description.txt#L31-L42)). GZIP
([RFC
1951](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1951)) and
ZSTD ([RFC
8878](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8878)) also
give common bytes shorter bit codes. On the plain
`city` column, SNAPPY cuts 3,299,981 bytes to
593,977. After dictionary encoding, little is left
to remove: 75,933 bytes become 75,957. The random
text of the `note` column barely shrinks with
SNAPPY. Its 13,340,241 encoded bytes become
12,872,675 compressed bytes, which is 3.5% less.
compress-bytes.wrapped_original_text:
Compress the Bytes
The writer then compresses each page with a codec ([specification](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/ec90dd4/Compression.md#L26-L29)), and the footer records the codec of each chunk. Every chunk in the example file uses SNAPPY, which is the default codec in pyarrow ([`write_table`](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/generated/pyarrow.parquet.write_table.html)). SNAPPY helps when bytes repeat ([format](https://github.com/google/snappy/blob/main/format_description.txt#L31-L42)). GZIP ([RFC 1951](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1951)) and ZSTD ([RFC 8878](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8878)) also give common bytes shorter bit codes. On the plain `city` column, SNAPPY cuts 3,299,981 bytes to 593,977. After dictionary encoding, little is left to remove: 75,933 bytes become 75,957. The random text of the `note` column barely shrinks with SNAPPY. Its 13,340,241 encoded bytes become 12,872,675 compressed bytes, which is 3.5% less.

row-group-skipping.wrapped_text:
Row Group Skipping
The footer stores the minimum and maximum
value of each column chunk ([`Statistics`](htt
ps://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/ec9
0dd4/src/main/thrift/parquet.thrift#L267-L311)
). A reader that filters on a column compares
the filter with these values. It skips every
row group that cannot match. In the example
file, `id` runs from 1 to 3 in row group 0 and
from 4 to 6 in row group 1. The filter `id >
3` keeps only row group 1.

Skipping works only when similar values sit in
the same row group. In the example, `fare`
runs from 8.0 to 20.0 in row group 0 and from
9.0 to 15.5 in row group 1. The filter `fare >
12` therefore keeps both. In the test file,
`id` is sorted, and `id >= 200000` keeps one
of three row groups. Its `fare` values are
random, so every row group runs from 5.0 to
60.0. The filter `fare > 55` keeps all three.
These results come from the pyarrow dataset
API in November 2026.

Snowflake tables use the same idea. Snowflake
keeps the range of values of each column for
each micro-partition. A query skips the
micro-partitions that cannot match ([micro-par
titions](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-gu
ide/tables-clustering-micropartitions)).
Apache Iceberg adds a level above the footer.
Each manifest records the minimum and maximum
value of each column for every data file. A
reader therefore skips whole files first. The
[Iceberg map](../iceberg/iceberg.md) describes
manifests. Inside each file that remains,
Iceberg's Parquet reader compares the footer
minimum and maximum values with the filter. It
skips row groups that cannot match ([`ReadConf
`](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/4616
acf/parquet/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/p
arquet/ReadConf.java#L94-L114)).

whole-rows-cost-more.wrapped_text:
Whole Rows Cost More
The column layout has a price. A row is spread
over every column. To rebuild one whole row, a
reader must read from every column of the row
group that holds it. In the test table,
fetching the row with `id` 250000 took SQLite
0.06 ms. Parquet needed 3.2 ms and 5,182,765
bytes, which is one row group and the footer.
CSV took 33 ms and scanned 16,335,389 bytes to
reach the row. SQLite is fast here because its
primary key leads to the page that holds the
whole row. Parquet suits queries that read
many rows of a few columns.

open-a-parquet-file.wrapped_text:
Open a Parquet File
A text editor shows a Parquet file as
unreadable characters. Tools that read Parquet
decode the bytes and show rows and columns:

- Snowflake: a stage is a named place for data
files, inside Snowflake or in cloud storage.
After you put the file in a stage, Snowflake
reads each Parquet row into one column, `$1`.
The query `SELECT $1:id, $1:city::varchar,
$1:fare FROM @my_stage/trips.parquet;` returns
the example columns ([Parquet tutorial](https:
//docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/tutorials/s
cript-data-load-transform-parquet)). The
function `INFER_SCHEMA` lists the column names
and types that the file stores ([`INFER_SCHEMA
`](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference
/functions/infer_schema)).
- pyarrow:
`pyarrow.parquet.read_table('trips.parquet')`
returns a table ([`read_table`](https://arrow.
apache.org/docs/python/generated/pyarrow.parqu
et.read_table.html)). Its `to_pydict()` method
returns the dictionary of columns.
- pandas, the Python data-analysis library:
`pandas.read_parquet('trips.parquet')` uses
pyarrow, or fastparquet if pyarrow is missing 
([`read_parquet`](https://pandas.pydata.org/do
cs/reference/api/pandas.read_parquet.html)).

files-are-written-once.wrapped_text:
Files Are Written Once
A writer creates a Parquet file in one pass,
and engines then leave it unchanged. To change
data, an engine writes a new file. This is a
habit of engines, and the layout makes it
practical. The format has no lock, and an
overwrite is possible.

The footer comes last, so a writer needs one
pass over the data ([specification](https://gi
thub.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/ec90dd4/RE
ADME.md#L109-L121)). The footer records the
byte range and the minimum and maximum value
of every chunk. These numbers describe the
exact bytes before the footer.

Experiments with pyarrow 18.1.0 in November
2026, on copies of the example file, show what
an overwrite does:

- Replace one value with another value of the
same size, in a copy written with plain
encoding and no compression. The file opens
and returns the new value, 99.0 in place of
20.0. The footer still says that the maximum
of `fare` is 20.0. The filter `fare > 50`
returns 0 rows when it uses the footer, and 1
row after a full read. Two readers give two
answers.
- Flip one byte inside a compressed chunk of
109 bytes. Of the 109 possible flips, 60 break
the read, 15 return different values without
an error, and 34 change nothing that a reader
sees.
- Insert one byte before a chunk. Every later
byte range in the footer is off by one, and
the read fails.
- Flip one byte in the footer. Of the 981
possible flips, 721 break the read.
- Add page checksums. A writer can store a
CRC32 checksum for each page ([specification](
https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/
ec90dd4/README.md#L224-L228)). With
`write_page_checksum=True` when writing and
`page_checksum_verification=True` when
reading, pyarrow reports the same-size edit as
an error: CRC checksum verification failed.

A table format such as Apache Iceberg tracks
which files are current. The [Iceberg
map](../iceberg/iceberg.md) describes its data
files as immutable.

tiny-files-waste-space.wrapped_text:
Tiny Files Waste Space
Every Parquet file carries its own footer. The
example file spends 981 of its 1,595 bytes on
the footer, which is more than the 602 bytes
of column data. The test file spends 1,893 of
its 15,353,361 bytes, which is 0.01%. A reader
also makes one extra read for each file, to
get the footer. Many tiny files therefore
waste storage and time.

Snowflake and Iceberg give sizes to aim for.
Snowflake recommends data files of roughly 100
to 250 MB compressed for loading ([loading gui
de](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/d
ata-load-considerations-prepare)). For a
Snowflake-managed Iceberg table, the setting
`TARGET_FILE_SIZE` sets a target Parquet file
size. The choices are `AUTO`, 16 MB, 32 MB, 64
MB, and 128 MB ([`CREATE ICEBERG TABLE`](https
://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/sql/cre
ate-iceberg-table-snowflake)). A streaming
writer can leave small files when it commits
often. The Iceberg sink connector in the
[Kafka → Iceberg → Snowflake map](../integrati
on/kafka-iceberg-snowflake/kafka-iceberg-snowf
lake.md) commits on a timer. Each of its tasks
writes its own Parquet files. Compaction in
Iceberg rewrites many small files into fewer
large ones. The [Iceberg
map](../iceberg/iceberg.md) describes it.

about-the-numbers.wrapped_text:
About the Numbers
The numbers in this map come from files that
scripts generated in November 2026. The example
file `trips.parquet` is stored beside this map, in
the folder `mind-maps/de/parquet/` of the mind-map
repository. The script below writes it again and
also creates the test file `trips_big.parquet`. Run
the script in an empty folder, because it writes
both files to the current folder. It uses [pyarrow]
(https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/generated/pya
rrow.parquet.write_table.html) 18.1.0:

```python
import random

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

example = pa.table(
{
"id": pa.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], pa.int64()),
"city": ["Perth", "Perth", "Sydney", "Sydney",
"Perth", "Perth"],
"fare": [12.5, 8.0, 20.0, 15.5, 9.0, 11.0],
}
)
pq.write_table(example, "trips.parquet",
row_group_size=3)

rng = random.Random(42)
n = 300_000
cities = ["Perth", "Sydney", "Melbourne",
"Brisbane"]
letters = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789"
test = pa.table(
{
"id": pa.array(range(n), pa.int64()),
"city": [rng.choice(cities) for _ in range(n)],
"fare": [round(rng.uniform(5, 60), 2) for _ in
range(n)],
"note": ["".join(rng.choices(letters, k=40)) for _
in range(n)],
}
)
pq.write_table(test, "trips_big.parquet",
row_group_size=100_000)
```

The example file `trips.parquet` holds the six rows
of the example table in two row groups of three
rows. It takes 1,595 bytes. The test file
`trips_big.parquet` holds 300,000 rows in three row
groups of 100,000 rows. It takes 15,353,361 bytes.
Other writers make files of other sizes.

The CSV file is the test table written with
`pyarrow.csv.write_csv`, which puts text in quotes.
It takes 19,625,110 bytes. The SQLite file holds
the same rows in the table `t (id INTEGER PRIMARY
KEY, city TEXT, fare REAL, note TEXT)`. It takes
20,017,152 bytes. Each query ran in Python on one
thread, with pyarrow and the `sqlite3` module. The
Parquet queries used the footer statistics to
choose row groups.

The width test wrote 100,000 rows of decimal
numbers with the expression `round(rng.uniform(0,
100), 2)` from `random.Random(7)`. The columns are
`c0`, `c1`, and so on, and the row groups have
50,000 rows.

The compression sizes compare columns of the test
table. Each CSV column is written with
`pyarrow.csv.write_csv` and compressed with ZSTD
through `pyarrow.compress`. Each Parquet column
comes from `pyarrow.parquet.write_table` with
`compression="zstd"`. The `city` and `fare` columns
use dictionary encoding. The `id` column uses
`column_encoding={"id": "DELTA_BINARY_PACKED"}`,
with `use_dictionary` listing the other columns.
The whole-table sizes compare the whole CSV file
with the whole Parquet file under the same codec.
The one-column read sums `fare` from a
ZSTD-compressed CSV file and from the Parquet file,
with the method of the queries above. The estimates
in the text round these results.

savings-depend-on-values.wrapped_text:
Savings Depend on Column Values
Parquet is efficient with compression for
three reasons. The writer encodes each column
by its type before the codec runs. The writer
picks the encoding and the codec for each
column, and the footer records both. A reader
decompresses only the pages of the columns
that a query needs.

The sizes below are rough. They come from the
test table with ZSTD as the codec. Each one
compares a Parquet column with the CSV text of
the same column, compressed with ZSTD too:

- Four different city names: about 4 times
smaller. Dictionary encoding does this.
- Ids that rise by one: thousands of times
smaller. Delta encoding stores only the step
between neighbours, which is always 1.
- Decimal fares: about 1.3 times smaller.
- Random letters: about the same size. Only
the codec can shrink them, by about a third
with ZSTD and a few percent with SNAPPY.

With ZSTD, the whole table is about half its
CSV size, in Parquet and in CSV alike. Parquet
is only a few percent smaller than the
compressed CSV, because two thirds of the
table is random letters. A query on one column
decompresses about 20 times fewer bytes than a
compressed CSV file needs, and it runs about
30 times faster.

Snowflake compresses each column of a
micro-partition on its own and picks the
algorithm itself ([micro-partitions](https://d
ocs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/tables-cluster
ing-micropartitions)). Iceberg writes Parquet
files with ZSTD unless the table property
`write.parquet.compression-codec` says
otherwise ([configuration](https://iceberg.apa
che.org/docs/latest/configuration/)).
